title: Not many wise, but not none
source_text: Τάχα δὲ καὶ ἐκ τοῦ „βλέπετε δὲ τὴν κλῆσιν ὑμῶν, ἀδελφοὶ, ὅτι οὐ πολλοὶ σοφοὶ κατὰ σάρκα, οὐ πολλοὶ δυνατοὶ, οὐ πολλοὶ εὐγενεῖς· ἀλλὰ τὰ μωρὰ τοῦ κόσμου ἐξελέξατο ὁ θεὸς. ἵνα καταισχύνῃ τοὺς σοφοὺς, καὶ τὰ ἀγενῆ καὶ τὰ ἐξουθενημένα ἐξελέξατο ὁ θεὸς καὶ τὰ μὴ ὄντα, ἵνα τὰ ὄντα καταργήσῃ, ἵνα μὴ καυχήσηται πᾶσα σὰρξ ἐνώπιον αὐτοῦ“ ἐκινήθησάν τινες πρὸς τὸ οἴεσθαι ὅτι οὐδεὶς πεπαιδευμένος ἢ σοφὸς ἢ φρόνιμος προσέρχεται τῷ λόγῳ. καὶ πρὸς τὸν τοιοῦτον δὲ φήσομεν ὅτι οὐκ εἴρηται ὅτι οὐδεὶς σοφὸς „κατὰ σάρκα,“ ἀλλ᾿ „οὐ πολλοὶ σοφοὶ κατὰ σάρκα.“ καὶ δῆλον ὅτι ἐν τῷ χαρακτηριστικῷ τῶν καλουμένων ἐπισκόπων διαγράφων ὁ Παῦλος, ὁποῖον εἶναι χρὴ τὸν ἐπίσκοπον, ἔταξε καὶ τὸν διδάσκαλον, λέγων δεῖν αὐτὸν εἶναι δυνατὸν „καὶ τοὺς ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν,“ ἵνα τοὺς ματαιολόγους καὶ φρεναπάτας ἐπιστομίζῃ διὰ τῆς ἐν αὐτῷ σοφίας. καὶ ὥσπερ μονόγαμον μᾶλλον διγάμου αἱρεῖται εἰς ἐπισκοπὴν καὶ „ἀνεπίληπτον“ ἐπιλήπτου καὶ „νηφάλιον“ τοῦ μὴ τοιούτου καὶ „σώφρονα“ τοῦ μὴ σώφρονος καὶ „κόσμιον“ παρὰ τὸν κἂν ἐπ᾿ ὀλίγον ἄκοσμον, οὕτως θέλει τὸν προηγουμένως εἰς ἐπισκοπὴν κατασταθησόμενον εἶναι διδακτικὸν καὶ δυνατὸν πρὸς τὸ „τοὺς ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν.“ πῶς οὖν εὐλόγως ἐγκαλεῖ ὁ Κέλσος ἡμῖν ὡς φάσκουσι· μηδεὶς προσίτω πεπαιδευμένος. μηδεὶς σοφὸς. μηδεὶς φρόνιμος; ἀλλὰ προσίτω μὲν πεπαιδευμένος καὶ σοφὸς καὶ φρόνιμος ὁ βουλόμενος· οὐδὲν δ᾿ ἧττον προσίτω καὶ εἴ τις ἀμαθὴς καὶ ἀνόητος καὶ ἀπαίδευτος καὶ νήπιος. καὶ γὰρ τοὺς τοιούτους προσελθόντας ἐπαγγέλλεται θεραπεύειν ὁ λόγος, πάντας ἀξίους κατασκευάζων τοῦ θεοῦ.
pass_a_gloss: Perhaps (τάχα) also from the [saying] 'see (βλέπετε) your calling (κλῆσιν), brothers, that not many wise according to flesh, not many powerful (δυνατοί), not many well-born (εὐγενεῖς); but the foolish things (τὰ μωρά) of the world God chose (ἐξελέξατο) so that he might shame (καταισχύνῃ) the wise, and the ignoble (ἀγενῆ) and the despised God chose, and the things that are not (τὰ μὴ ὄντα), so that he might abolish (καταργήσῃ) the things that are, so that all flesh may not boast (καυχήσηται) before him' some were moved (ἐκινήθησαν) to think that no one educated or wise (σοφός) or sensible (φρόνιμος) comes to (προσέρχεται) the word (λόγῳ). And to such a one we shall say that it is not said 'no one wise according to flesh' but 'not many wise according to flesh'. And it is clear that in the characterization of those called bishops (ἐπισκόπων), Paul, sketching (διαγράφων) what sort the bishop must be, appointed (ἔταξε) him also teacher (διδάσκαλον), saying he must be able 'also to refute (ἐλέγχειν) those who speak against (ἀντιλέγοντας)', so that he may muzzle (ἐπιστομίζῃ) the vain talkers (ματαιολόγους) and mind-deceivers (φρεναπάτας) through the wisdom in him. And as he chooses (αἱρεῖται) for oversight (ἐπισκοπήν) a once-married man (μονόγαμον) rather than a twice-married (διγάμου), and 'irreproachable' (ἀνεπίληπτον) over the reproachable, and 'sober' (νηφάλιον) over one not such, and 'self-controlled' (σώφρονα) over the not self-controlled, and 'orderly' (κόσμιον) beside one even a little disorderly (ἄκοσμον), so he wants the one principally (προηγουμένως) to be appointed to oversight to be apt to teach (διδακτικόν) and able 'to refute those who speak against'. How then does Celsus reasonably (εὐλόγως) accuse (ἐγκαλεῖ) us as saying: let no educated person approach (προσίτω), no wise, no sensible? Rather let approach the educated and wise and sensible, whoever wishes; but no less let approach also anyone ignorant (ἀμαθής), senseless (ἀνόητος), uneducated (ἀπαίδευτος), infant (νήπιος). For the word promises (ἐπαγγέλλεται) to heal (θεραπεύειν) such ones also when they have come, making (κατασκευάζων) all worthy (ἀξίους) of God.
pass_b_english: Perhaps, too, some have been led by the words, “Consider your calling, brothers: not many were wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many of noble birth; but God chose the foolish things of the world to put the wise to shame; and God chose the low-born things and the despised things, and the things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are, so that no flesh might boast before him” (1 Corinthians 1:26–29), to suppose that no one educated or wise or sensible comes to the word.

To such a person we shall reply that it does not say “no one wise according to the flesh,” but “not many wise according to the flesh.” And it is clear that when Paul, in his sketch of those called bishops, describes what kind of man the bishop must be, he also made him a teacher, saying that he must be able “also to refute those who contradict” (Titus 1:9), so that by the wisdom in him he may stop the mouths of empty talkers and deceivers (Titus 1:10–11). And just as for the office of bishop he prefers a man married once to one married twice, the “blameless” to the blameworthy, the “sober” to one who is not, the “self-controlled” to one who lacks self-control, and the “orderly” to one who is even slightly disorderly (1 Timothy 3:2), so he wants the man who is to be appointed bishop to be, above all, apt to teach (1 Timothy 3:2) and able “to refute those who contradict” (Titus 1:9).

How, then, can Celsus reasonably accuse us of saying, “Let no educated person come, no wise person, no sensible person”? No: let the educated, wise and sensible person come, whoever wishes; but let anyone who is ignorant, foolish, uneducated or childish come no less. For the word promises to heal such people too when they come, making all worthy of God.

choices.choice: 1 Corinthians 1:26-29 as Origen quotes it lacks verse 27b ('and God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong'); translated as the Greek stands, not supplied. The bishop list (once married, blameless, sober, self-controlled, orderly, apt to teach) follows 1 Timothy 3:2 (cf. Titus 1:6-7); 'refute those who contradict' is Titus 1:9; 'empty talkers and deceivers' and 'stop the mouths' allude to Titus 1:10-11 (Greek ματαιολόγοι καὶ φρεναπάται; ἐπιστομίζειν). 'Above all' renders προηγουμένως, which sits with the participle 'the one to be appointed'; it could also mean 'the one to be appointed by preference'. The words 'Let no educated person come...' are Celsus's (quoted at 3.44, where he puts them in the mouths of Christians); Origen repeats them as a charge, so they stand in quotation marks.
Reordered the last clause of Origen's reply into natural English ('let anyone who is ignorant ... come no less'); sense unchanged.
Checked 1 Corinthians 1:26-29 (27b missing in Origen's text, as noted), Titus 1:9, Titus 1:10-11 and 1 Timothy 3:2 against the verses; all correct.
